ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, the line $l: y=k_{1}x+b$ intersects with the hyperbola $y=\frac{k_{2}}{x}(x>0)$ at points A and B, and intersects with the x-axis at point C. If the x-coordinates of points A and B are 1 and 2 respectively, please directly provide the solution set of $k_{1}x+b>\frac{k_{2}}{x}$.
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:} From the given problem, we have $k_{1}x+b>\frac{k_{2}}{x}$,\\
the solution set is $x\in(1,2)$,\\
$\therefore$ the solution set is $x\in\boxed{(1,2)}$.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure there is a rectangular coordinate system; in the right half-plane, a straight line l slanting downward to the right is drawn, as well as a decreasing hyperbola located in the region x>0. The straight line l intersects the hyperbola at two points A and B, and continues downward to intersect the x-axis at point C. It can be seen from the figure that, within the segment of the range between the two intersection points A and B, the straight line l is above the hyperbola. Reasoning: The problem gives that the abscissas of the two points A and B are 1 and 2, respectively. To solve k_1x+b>k_2/x is to find the range of abscissas where the function value of the straight line y=k_1x+b is greater than that of the hyperbola y=k_2/x. According to the image, the straight line is higher than the hyperbola between the two intersection points; since it is the inequality sign “>”, the intersection points are not included. Therefore the solution set is 1<x<2.
